name: Tóth Árpád Promenade
description: A tree-lined walk along the castle wall in Buda Castle District, laid out on the line of an old defensive passage. It looks out toward the Buda hills, Tabán and Gellért Hill, carries the name of the poet Árpád Tóth, and is known for the Japanese ornamental cherries that bloom along it in spring.

children.text: The Tóth Árpád Promenade (Tóth Árpád sétány) runs along the castle wall on the western side of the Buda Castle District. Time Out Budapest describes it as a route with centuries of history that began as a defensive passage and later became a walkway. Today it is a quiet, green stretch of the district that most visitors use as a slow alternative to the busier squares around Matthias Church.

The views are the main reason to come. Visit Buda Castle speaks of vistas toward the Buda hills and the city, while Time Out highlights the outlook over the Tabán district and Gellért Hill. In spring, Japanese ornamental cherry trees blossom along the path, and both sources single this season out as the most photogenic time to walk it.

The name is more recent than the walkway. According to a Hungarian city-culture article, the area behind the castle wall was occupied by gardens until 1936, when they were cleared and the Bástya sétány (Bastion Promenade) was created. In the second half of the 1960s that promenade was divided into sections, and the Tóth Árpád sétány is one half of the former Bástya sétány. It is named after the poet Árpád Tóth (1886-1928), a lyric poet associated with the Nyugat circle; the Castle District heritage site says the lane received its present name in 1946. None of the pages consulted explains why he was chosen.

Along the walk you can find a statue of Artúr Görgei at the Fehérvári rondella, according to Time Out, and the promenade is within a few minutes of Dísz tér, the Vienna Gate (Bécsi kapu) and the Fisherman's Bastion. Visit Buda Castle also places it near Kapisztrán tér and the Military History Institute and Museum, which makes it an easy addition to a Castle District day.
Good to know
Spring, when the ornamental cherry trees bloom, is the season both Time Out and Visit Buda Castle recommend for the promenade.
Time Out suggests starting at the Castle, walking down toward Tabán and finishing near Gellért Hill.
Dísz tér, the Vienna Gate and the Fisherman's Bastion are all a few minutes' walk away, so the promenade combines well with a Castle District visit.

historyIntro: The promenade along the western castle wall began as a defensive passage and became a public walk, taking its present name in the 20th century. The documented record is thin, and the sources read give few dates.

historySections.heading: A defensive passage on the wall

children.text: Time Out Budapest describes the Tóth Árpád Promenade as a route with a history of several centuries that grew out of a former defensive passage along the castle wall, on the western side of the Castle District. The page gives no construction dates and does not say who built the passage or when it first became a place for walking. The English Wikipedia article on Buda Castle describes a reconstruction of the castle's fortifications from the 1950s to 1966, and its article on the Bastion Promenade says the promenade was heavily damaged in the Second World War and rebuilt between 1966 and 1970.

historySections.heading: From Bástya sétány to a named promenade

children.text: A Hungarian city-culture article records that in 1936 gardens still occupied the ground behind the wall, and that they were removed to make way for the Bástya sétány, the Bastion Promenade. In the second half of the 1960s that promenade was cut into several sections. The Tóth Árpád sétány is described as the other half of the former Bástya sétány, while the Babits Mihály sétány came from the same division. The promenade now bears the name of the poet Árpád Tóth, who lived from 1886 to 1928 and wrote for the journal Nyugat. The pages consulted do not explain why he was chosen.

name: Garden of Philosophers
description: A small sculpture garden on the side of Gellért Hill, where eight life-size bronze figures by Nándor Wagner face a shared centre. Religious founders and thinkers stand together in a work meant to show what cultures have in common. It was a gift from the sculptor's widow and was unveiled in 2001.

children.text: The Garden of Philosophers (Filozófusok kertje) is a quiet sculpture group on the western side of Gellért Hill, between Orom utca and Hegyalja út and behind the Rudas Baths. It is the work of the sculptor Nándor Wagner, and Visit Buda Castle describes it as an eight-figure group that highlights values which religions and cultures share. The life-size bronze figures face each other, looking toward the geometric centre of the group.

A guide from the XpatLoop site names the figures. Five stand in a ring around a sunken pool: Abraham, Jesus, Buddha, Laozi and Akhenaten. Abraham is the only one not standing, and crouches with his head in his hands. Behind the ring stand Mahatma Gandhi, Bodhidharma and Saint Francis of Assisi. Each figure focuses on a small globe, which the guide says represents divine essence. Wikipedia describes Wagner's wider concept as having a further ring of lawgivers, but the Budapest sources describe eight figures, which is what stands here.

Wagner was born in Oradea in 1922 and left Hungary after the 1956 revolution, living first in Sweden and then in Japan, where he died in 1997. According to Wikipedia he conceived the work in Mashiko, Japan, as a spiritual message for future generations. The Budapest set was a gift from his widow and was unveiled on Gellért Hill on 18 October 2001. XpatLoop adds that the architect István Makk, who had known Wagner and visited him in Japan in 1995, chose the site.

The group has had a difficult history. Hungarian magazine HVG reported in 2007 that three of the bronzes, depicting Gandhi, Saint Francis and Bodhidharma (named Dharma in the article), had been stolen after an earlier attempt the previous October that damaged the figures. The article notes that plaster moulds for recasting exist in Japan. Közterkép and a Budapest city blog report that the three figures were later recast from moulds provided by Wagner's widow and that the full set of eight was back in place by 2010. A separate small sculpture of Prince Buda and Princess Pest stands nearby.
Good to know
The garden lies on a hillside between Orom utca and Hegyalja út, behind the Rudas Baths, so expect an uphill walk from the riverside.
Three figures were stolen in 2007, but they were recast and the full set of eight was back in place by 2010, and a 2023 guide describes all eight.
It combines naturally with a visit to the Rudas Baths and the other sights on Gellért Hill.

historyIntro: The Garden of Philosophers on Gellért Hill is a bronze sculpture group created by Nándor Wagner and given to Budapest by his widow. It was unveiled in October 2001 and has been damaged by thieves since.

historySections.heading: Wagner and the idea of a philosophical garden

children.text: Nándor Wagner was born in Oradea in 1922 and studied at the Budapest art academy. After the suppression of the 1956 revolution he was admitted to Sweden, where he worked in Lund, and later settled in Mashiko in Japan, where he met his wife, the art student Chiyo. According to Wikipedia he created the Garden of Philosophy there as a spiritual message for present and future generations and said it was not made to earn money. XpatLoop reports that he unveiled the first statue, Laozi, in 1977 and the others during the 1980s in Japan.

historySections.heading: A gift to Budapest, unveiled in 2001

children.text: Wagner died in 1997. Wikipedia says three sets were cast, for Japan, Hungary and the United States, and that the Hungarian set was unveiled on Gellért Hill on 18 October 2001. The Hungarian magazine HVG describes the Budapest group as a gift from the sculptor's widow, and XpatLoop adds that the architect István Makk, who had known Wagner and visited him in Japan in 1995, chose the site. The Budapest sources describe eight life-size bronze figures facing a shared centre.

HVG reported in April 2007 that three of the bronzes, depicting Gandhi, Saint Francis and Bodhidharma, were stolen from the hill, with damage estimated at about thirty million forints, according to the director of the Budapest Gallery. The article says that the previous October someone had removed five large bronze arc pieces that stood around the statues and had cut notches in the figures with a saw so that they could be broken off, but that an eyewitness interrupted them. It also notes that plaster moulds for recasting the statues exist in Japan. Közterkép says the three figures were recast in Japan in 2009 from moulds provided by Wagner's widow, and a Budapest city blog says the Budapest and Buda Castle district municipalities paid for the replacements, which completed the group again by 2010.

name: Cave Church
description: A church built into natural and artificial caves on the side of Gellért Hill, linked to the Pauline order. Founded after Hungarian pilgrims visited Lourdes in the 1920s, it was walled up under communism and reopened as that era ended; thermal water keeps the interior mild.

children.text: The Cave Church is built into the southeastern side of Gellért Hill, partly in a natural cave and partly in man-made chambers. Visit Buda Castle describes it as set in natural and artificial cave cavities and links it to the Pauline order. Visitors enter an outer cave and then follow a tunnel-like corridor to the deeper man-made church, where Masses and prayers are held. Visit Hungary says hot springs through the hill keep the interior at about 20 degrees Celsius all year.

The church grew out of a pilgrimage. According to We Love Budapest and Visit Hungary, Hungarian pilgrims who visited Lourdes in the 1920s proposed building a cave chapel inspired by the grotto there. We Love Budapest says it was consecrated in 1926, with the main altar in the outer cave and benches on the rock terrace outside; Visit Hungary gives 1931 as the year the construction was completed, so the sources differ. A legend recorded by We Love Budapest tells of a hermit named Iván who healed the sick with the bubbling waters at the cave's entrance.

In 1934 the Pauline order returned to Hungary after about 150 years in exile, bringing sixteen monks from Poland, according to We Love Budapest. Volunteers enlarged the cave with controlled explosions, and a neo-Romanesque monastery was built on the Danube side of the hill. During the Second World War the Pauline fathers sheltered civilians and refugees, sometimes disguising them as monks.

Under communist rule the monastic orders were abolished, the monks were forced out, the entrance was walled up with concrete and the cross above it was torn down. Sources differ on the date: We Love Budapest says the wall dates to 1960, Visit Hungary says only the 1950s, and Wikipedia and Aleteia say the cave was sealed in 1951. The wall was demolished as communist rule ended (Wikipedia gives 1989, Visit Hungary the 1990s), and the Pauline order restored the church. A section of the wall still stands on the right side of the entrance as a reminder.

Inside, the features named by the two sources include a bronze altar with a Polish eagle, a green pyrogranite altar made by the Zsolnay manufactory, a statue of Our Lady of Lourdes, a statue of Saint Stephen at the entrance and a ceramic relief of Saint Gellért. A relic believed to be part of the tibia of Saint Paul the Hermit, the Pauline order's most important relic, is also kept here.
Good to know
This is an active place of worship where Masses and prayers are held, so be considerate of worshippers.
Check the official Pauline Cave Church page for current visiting arrangements and the times and languages of services.
Look at the right side of the entrance for the preserved section of the concrete wall from the communist era.
The church is set in the side of Gellért Hill, so it combines naturally with other sights on the hill.

historyIntro: Budapest's Cave Church is a striking place of worship cut into the rock of Gellért Hill, with a twentieth-century history of hardship and return.

historySections.heading: A church fashioned from the hillside

children.text: The Pauline order developed the cave church in the early twentieth century; the sources give 1926 for its consecration and 1931 for the completion of construction. The distinctive interior connects Christian worship with the natural rock of the hill above the Danube.

During the Second World War, monks provided refuge here to people in danger. The church was closed and sealed with a concrete wall in 1951, according to Wikipedia and Aleteia. The wall came down as communist rule ended, and sources date the reopening between 1989 and 1992.

stories.title: The hermit Iván and the healing waters

children.text: We Love Budapest records a legend of a hermit named Iván who healed the sick with the bubbling waters at the cave's entrance. This is a legend, not a documented event.
